A few months ago I decided to build a Linux gaming PC because I had a spare Dell with an i5 and an older Nvidia card and because the new Vulcan drivers had just come available and everyone was excited about them so I had to see what the fuss was all about. I had just switched to Manjaro and after a bit of research decided it was a good choice for this project. The experience went fantastically well and I don't hesitate to recommend Manjaro for a gaming. BUT just because it went well for me is no guarantee -- every PC is different and some Distros will run better than others. For example I've never had any luck installing Debian, but yet it's a very popular and respected Distro so rather than blame Debian I assume it's something about the PC.

In fact lot of people suggest going with Debian for gaming because SteamOS is based on it and because there are so many Linux games on Steam, but I have no idea if this is actually valid reasoning -- I mean it makes sense but I haven't read anything that actually supports it.

The other thing you'll be faced with is which DE (Desktop Environment) to chose. And this is perhaps as daunting a task for newcomers as picking a Distro. Some DEs definitely do some things better so if you have specific preferences it's probably worthwhile to do some research. Otherwise I heartily recommend you go with whatever the default DE is that comes with the Distro. You don't have to worry about making a mistake here because #1 installing multiple DEs is a snap, and #2 switching to a different installed DE is also a snap.

In the long run DEs, like Distros, are more about what you're comfortable with than which is the right one. So like I said don't get hung up initially over which one to start off with.

FWIW my DE on Manjaro is KDE Plasma 5.

Good luck. Coming over from Windows is easier than you think, but you'll think that only after you get there. You will have problems and set backs, but remember you can ask questions here. Regardless the answer to any virtually any question you'll have will have been answered by someone somewhere on the net so, as always, google is your friend.

For example I've never had any luck installing Debian, but yet it's a very popular and respected Distro so rather than blame Debian I assume it's something about the PC.

Those aren't the only two possibilities: It could also be the way you think. And no, I'm not calling you dumb! :) It's just that different distribution maintainers have different goals and ways of thinking. If you're not prone to making the same sort of decisions they would when building a distribution, you're not really on the same wavelength and you'll never quite jibe with their distro.

It's hard for me to say exactly what would make somebody not work with Debian well, but it could be related to their relatively slow adoption of new software or their devotion to the ideal of not using any closed-source code.

For what it's worth, I just cannot deal with rolling release distributions - you have to be a lot more careful when updating them, in my experience, as the automatic update scripts tend to clobber configurations and suddenly change the way the system works. Everybody's different.

I would recommend Ubuntu MATE or Peppermint 7. MATE has the software welcome center that lets you get used to the open source alternatives to the popular windows applications, and Peppermint focuses a lot on web apps (Google Drive, Calendar, Gmail) which will be immediately familiar to any Windows user who has migrated a lot of their work to the browser. KDE can be made very similar to Windows 7 with the cascading menus and icon only taskbar, but both Kubuntu 16.04 and KDE Neon (Kubuntu with more up to date desktop packages) seem to be causing headaches for people. I use KDE on Manjaro and love it, but I would not immediately recommend a rolling release to a new user.

You can't go wrong with any of the Ubuntu variants but give Manjaro a try. Its an Arch variant that takes a step back from the build it yourself style and gives you a complete easy to get use, abuse, break, and fix OS. It also has the benefit of oodles of Arch documentation as well as plenty of its own.
